findings.claim: Greater London dominates with 9.7 million people
findings.truth: Greater London held about 9.1 million people (ONS mid-2024 estimate, 9,089,736). The 9.7 million figure is the 2011 London built-up area, which is a different boundary.
findings.evidence: ONS mid-year estimate via Wikipedia, Greater London

findings.claim: The Midlands conurbation around Birmingham (4 million); repeated in L2 as 'around 4 million across the wider West Midlands conurbation'
findings.truth: The West Midlands conurbation (Birmingham, Wolverhampton, the Black Country, Solihull) holds about 2.44 million. The whole West Midlands metropolitan county holds about 3.04 million (2024). No boundary gives 4 million.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, West Midlands (county), citing census and ONS figures

findings.claim: Shanghai ... saw GDP per capita rise from $200 to over $25,000
findings.truth: $200 was China's national GDP per capita in 1980. Shanghai's was several times higher. The modern figure (about $26,000) is sound.
findings.evidence: World Bank national series; no settled Shanghai 1980 value found

findings.claim: Today the M6, M42 and M5 motorways converge at Spaghetti Junction
findings.truth: Spaghetti Junction (Gravelly Hill) is where the M6 meets the A38(M) Aston Expressway and local roads. The M5 joins the M6 at Ray Hall and the M42 at junction 4; neither passes through Spaghetti Junction.

findings.claim: Around 25% of the UK's manufacturing output still comes from this region.
findings.truth: The West Midlands produces roughly a tenth of UK manufacturing output. A quarter is far too high, and the source of the figure is unknown.

findings.claim: The inner city is a band of mid-Victorian housing untouched since 1900.
findings.truth: Inner Birmingham was largely cleared and rebuilt between 1950 and 1975; tower blocks and post-war estates sit among the surviving terraces.

findings.claim: Edexcel will give you 12 marks across the 'chosen UK city' section if you can name and locate features.
findings.truth: Invented mark allocation. This paper has three 30-mark sections and its longest question is 8 marks; 12-mark extended writing belongs only to the fieldwork and UK challenges paper.
findings.evidence: spec assessment overview, Component 2 and Component 3

findings.claim: examiners reward labelled diagrams
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim. No published mark scheme says this.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented examiner claims

findings.claim: EU enlargement in 2004 added a wave of Polish and Romanian migrants.
findings.truth: Romania joined the EU in 2007, not 2004. Only Poland and seven other states joined in 2004.

findings.claim: Child poverty in Ladywood reached around 47% in 2023, more than double the city average.
findings.truth: Birmingham's own child poverty rate is around 40%, well above the England average. A ward at 47% cannot be more than double the city average.
findings.evidence: End Child Poverty coalition local-authority figures; internal arithmetic

findings.claim: For 12-mark evaluations, weigh strategies against each other
findings.truth: There is no 12-mark question on this paper. The spec lists 12-mark extended writing only for the fieldwork and UK challenges paper.
findings.evidence: spec assessment overview, Component 2 versus Component 3

findings.claim: examiners reward precise place knowledge over generic urban theory
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented examiner claims

findings.claim: the named places and statistics needed for 8- and 12-mark questions
findings.truth: There is no 12-mark question on this paper.

findings.claim: the world's busiest container ports at Jawaharlal Nehru Port
findings.truth: Jawaharlal Nehru Port is India's busiest container port. It handles about 6 million containers a year and ranks far below Shanghai, Singapore and the other world leaders.

findings.claim: the underground Mumbai Metro
findings.truth: Most Mumbai Metro lines are elevated. Only Line 3 runs underground.

findings.claim: examiners want Mumbai-specific evidence in every paragraph
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim. The case-study requirement is real, but the examiner voice is invented.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented examiner claims

findings.claim: In 2022 the UK's GDP per capita was around $46,000 (US dollars, PPP-adjusted), Bangladesh's was around $7,300 and Norway's was around $82,000.
findings.truth: World Bank 2022 PPP values are UK $60,267, Bangladesh $8,449 and Norway $129,914. The $46,000 UK figure is the nominal value, so the three numbers were not on one measure.

findings.claim: Saudi Arabia (high GDP per capita, around $59,000 ...); repeated in the exam tip
findings.truth: World Bank 2022 PPP for Saudi Arabia is $71,957. Costa Rica at about $26,000 is correct ($26,892).

findings.claim: The 2024 HDI ranks Switzerland top (0.967) and Niger bottom (0.394); repeated in a practice mark scheme
findings.truth: In that report Somalia (0.380) and South Sudan (0.381) sit below Niger, which ranks 189th of 193. Niger was last in the 2020 report, not this one.

findings.claim: Norway's GDP per capita is around 35 times that of Burundi (also in the key fact)
findings.truth: World Bank 2022 PPP gives Norway $129,914 and Burundi $1,101, a gap of about 118 times. On nominal figures the gap is larger still. No measure gives 35.

findings.claim: the World Bank's funding of the Mumbai-Ahmedabad rail corridor
findings.truth: The Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed line is funded mainly by a Japanese (JICA) loan. The World Bank funded Mumbai's suburban rail through the Mumbai Urban Transport Project.
findings.evidence: project funding records for both schemes

findings.claim: The UK's GDP per capita varies from around 57,000 pounds in inner London
findings.truth: 57,000 pounds per head is the figure for the London region as a whole. Inner London West is several times higher, close to 200,000 pounds per head.

findings.claim: the UN Sustainable Development Goals (17 targets to 2030); the same wording in a knowledge check
findings.truth: The SDGs are 17 goals, divided into 169 targets.

findings.claim: contains the world's second-largest Muslim population
findings.truth: Indonesia, Pakistan and India are all close, and most current estimates put India third. The rank is disputed, so a rank-free wording is safer.

findings.claim: Total fertility has fallen from around 4.5 children per woman in 1990; repeated in a practice mark scheme
findings.truth: India's total fertility rate in 1990 was 4.05.

findings.claim: For 12-mark evaluations, structure as positive impacts, negative impacts, government response, judgement
findings.truth: There is no 12-mark question on this paper.

findings.claim: reduced biodiversity (Amazon deforestation around 10 million hectares a year globally)
findings.truth: 10 million hectares a year is global forest loss. Amazon loss runs at roughly 1 to 2 million hectares a year. As written the sentence attaches the global figure to the Amazon.

findings.claim: Sitka spruce plantations cover around 13% of the UK; the same claim in a flashcard
findings.truth: 13% is total UK woodland cover (about 3.25 million hectares). Sitka spruce makes up roughly a quarter of that, near 3% of UK land.

findings.claim: Around 70% of the EU's overall water footprint comes from goods imported from beyond its borders.
findings.truth: About 70% is the UK's external water footprint. The EU's external share is nearer 40%.
findings.evidence: WWF UK water footprint work; Water Footprint Network EU figures

findings.claim: Renewables and low-carbon together provided over half of UK electricity for the first time.
findings.truth: Renewables plus nuclear passed half of UK electricity several years before 2023. The 2023 share of about 56% was not a first.
findings.evidence: UK electricity generation mix by year

findings.claim: Hinkley Point C ... is set to add 3.2 GW from 2027 (delayed from 2025); the same date in a flashcard
findings.truth: EDF moved the start of the first reactor to between 2029 and 2031 in January 2024. The 3.2 GW capacity is right.
findings.evidence: EDF Hinkley Point C schedule revision, January 2024

findings.claim: The government plans to ban new petrol and diesel cars by 2035.
findings.truth: The 2030 date was restored, with some hybrids allowed until 2035. The 2035 date alone is out of date.
findings.evidence: UK zero emission vehicle phase-out policy

findings.claim: The London Pollard Switch Off campaign
findings.truth: No such campaign exists. It is a fabricated named example. The 2022 hosepipe bans across southern England are a real substitute.

findings.claim: Every lesson carries a '6 marks - Explain Causes & Impacts' practice question, and four exam tips coach '6-mark questions'.
findings.truth: The spec lists this paper's question types as multiple-choice, short open, open response, calculations and 8-mark extended writing. A 6-mark item is not ruled out (it would be open response) but it is not named, and the checker brief treats a 6-mark tier as another board's form. The ladder 1/2/3/4/6/8 is used across the whole geography corpus, so this is a corpus decision, not a unit fix. Options: (a) leave the ladder alone, (b) retire the 6-mark tier corpus-wide and split it into 4 and 8.
findings.ruling: Leave (corpus-level tariff ruling / unverified series / attribution unverified).

findings.claim: Global water use has roughly doubled since 1975 (repeated in the conclusion, a flashcard and a practice mark scheme, which also says agricultural use 'roughly doubled in volume' 1975-2025)
findings.truth: Global freshwater withdrawals have risen by roughly 40 to 50% since 1975, not doubled; the UN puts growth near 1% a year. The share statement in the same mark scheme (agriculture falling from about 80% to about 70%) is sound. Recommended ruling: change 'roughly doubled' to 'risen by about half' in all four places. Held back because the sources permitted here do not carry the withdrawal series.
findings.evidence: UN World Water Development Report growth rate; FAO AQUASTAT series not fetchable within the allowed sources
findings.ruling: Leave (corpus-level tariff ruling / unverified series / attribution unverified).

findings.claim: Wakal River Basin, Rajasthan (developing) has used WaterAid bottom-up projects to build small earth dams and stone johads
findings.truth: The Wakal River Basin scheme is normally credited to local NGOs rather than to WaterAid. The scheme itself, the johads and the 5-10 m rise in groundwater are sound. Recommended ruling: drop the charity name and keep the rest.
findings.evidence: no source found linking WaterAid to the Wakal scheme
findings.ruling: Leave (corpus-level tariff ruling / unverified series / attribution unverified).

findings.claim: by 1830 the city had 174 km of canals - more than Venice (also in a knowledge check stem)
findings.truth: No published figure matches. The Birmingham Canal Navigations peaked at about 257 km and about 160 km stay navigable; Birmingham itself has about 56 km. The 'more than Venice' comparison holds on any of these.

findings.claim: New Street handles 53 million passenger journeys a year
findings.truth: That is a pre-pandemic total including interchanges. Recent ORR data give about 39 million entries and exits. The claim that New Street is the busiest station outside London still holds.

findings.claim: The 2021 Census recorded a city population of 1.14 million, the largest since 1971.
findings.truth: Birmingham's 1971 population was about 1.01 million, lower than 2021, so the wording implies a fall that did not happen. Boundary changes in 1974 make a clean 'highest ever' claim hard to state.

findings.claim: around 735 million people went hungry in 2023 according to the UN
findings.truth: 735 million is the 2022 figure; the UN reported 733 million for 2023. The number is right, the year is a step behind.
findings.evidence: UN State of Food Security and Nutrition reports

findings.claim: $36 billion of foreign direct investment flowing in during 2023
findings.truth: Published figures differ widely by definition: UNCTAD puts net inflows near $28 billion, India's own gross figure is near $71 billion. $36 billion matches neither.

findings.claim: diaspora communities of over 18 million in the UK, the United States and the Gulf
findings.truth: 18 million is India's whole global diaspora, the largest in the world, not the total for those three destinations.

findings.claim: North Sea oil and gas ... supply around 30% of UK gas demand (also in a flashcard)
findings.truth: Recent UK production has met closer to half of demand. The figure could not be settled from the sources permitted here.
findings.evidence: DESNZ gas production and demand series, not fetchable within the allowed sources

findings.claim: an average North American uses around 200 litres a day for domestic purposes
findings.truth: US household use is usually given as 300 litres or more per person per day. The UK average is about 140 litres.
findings.evidence: US EPA and Waterwise household use figures

findings.claim: the world used around 25 times more primary energy in 2023 than in 1924
findings.truth: Long-run energy series suggest a rise nearer 15 times. The direction of the point is sound.

findings.claim: Greater Manchester/Merseyside 2.8m, Yorkshire 2m, the Central Belt 1.7m
findings.truth: Each is boundary-dependent and none is clearly wrong: Greater Manchester alone is 2.9 million, West Yorkshire 2.4 million, and the whole Central Belt about 3.5 million. Left alone because no single true value applies.
findings.evidence: ONS mid-year estimates for metropolitan counties

summary: All ten lessons carry findings: 32 FIX (4 HIGH, 25 MEDIUM, 3 LOW), 3 ADJUDICATE and 11 NOTE, delivered as 45 edits. The two systematic faults are exam claims borrowed from the fieldwork paper (three lessons coach 12-mark questions that do not exist on this paper, plus one invented 12-mark allocation and four fabricated examiner claims) and stale or mislabelled statistics (Greater London, the West Midlands conurbation, five GDP per capita figures, India's 1990 fertility rate, Hinkley Point C, the petrol and diesel ban). One named example is fabricated outright: the 'London Pollard Switch Off campaign'.
